generation.final_prompt:
Rendering style:
Create an authored editorial illustration for a serious technology newspaper.

Direction:
- authored editorial print language
- deliberate simplified shapes with clear focal hierarchy
- restrained limited palette
- subtle physical print texture
- controlled abstraction and strong negative space
- non-photorealistic but factually grounded representation
- newspaper and social-card readability

Fixed factual and safety restrictions:
- Do not render visible text, captions, headlines, or newspaper typography.
- Do not render logos or trademarks.
- Do not fabricate visible factual evidence.
- Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
- Do not imitate a named or living artist.

Profile-specific exclusions:
- glossy CGI
- luxury product render
- generic futuristic concept art
- cyberpunk or neon
- glowing circuit-board decoration
- floating particles
- heroic centered hardware
- server rack treated as monument or skyscraper
- generic server room
- advertising composition
- airbrushed gradients
- synthetic chrome
- excessive pseudo-technical detail
- malformed or visible text
- labels
- diagrams with words

Exact source facts:
Title: STRIPE AND SIERRA BUILT THEIR OWN CODING AGENT SYSTEMS. YOU PROBABLY DON'T NEED TO
Summary: Most companies should buy coding-agent infrastructure and focus their resources on the context and workflows that make it uniquely valuable. Building internally is worthwhile only when the technology is strategically essential, and the organization can support it as a permanent product.

Editorial idea:
The strategic choice between buying coding-agent infrastructure and building it internally depends on whether the organization can make its own context and workflows a lasting advantage.

Central subject:
A standardized tool being adapted to a distinctive working process

Visual relationship:
An off-the-shelf implement fits into a carefully shaped workbench, while a separate unfinished custom mechanism sits beside it, showing the contrast between adopting infrastructure and sustaining an internal build.

Composition:
A clear workbench viewed from above: the ready-made implement is aligned with a set of organization-specific templates and procedures, while the custom mechanism is only partly assembled at the edge. The finished workflow receives the visual emphasis, not the tools themselves.

Permitted literal elements:
A finished implement
A partly assembled mechanism
Distinctive workflow templates
A workbench with organized materials

Abstraction level:
medium

Story-specific forbidden elements:
Server racks
Computer chips
Laptops
Clouds
Robots
Shields
Arrows
Charts
Skyscrapers
Chess
Handshakes
Split-screen conflict
Logos
Rendered text

Likely failure modes to avoid:
Suggesting that building internally is always inferior
Showing generic software hardware without the buy-versus-build relationship
Making the custom mechanism appear broken rather than costly to maintain
Adding unsupported technical components

Global factual restrictions:
Do not fabricate visible factual evidence. Do not imitate a named or living artist. Do not render interfaces or screenshots.
Do not render any words, letters, numbers, labels, captions, annotations, signage, diagrams with text, logos, watermarks, or pseudo-writing anywhere in the image.
If the concept cannot be represented without visible text, represent the relationship through shape, scale, spacing, direction, grouping, interruption, containment, or contrast instead.
